title: Inference-Time Scaling of Discrete Diffusion Models via Importance Weighting and Optimal Proposal Design
claim: A sampling-based controller steers a base generative distribution to concentrate on reward-tilted or product-of-experts targets, showing the method hits the intended distributions.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter panels with overlaid legends; left shows a 3x3 grid of clusters with the reward-tilted mode in the center row, right shows four corner clusters with product-target overlap; the cropped importance-weight equation (7) runs across the top
description: The figure shows two 2-D scatter plots of sample clouds, set under a cropped fragment of an importance-weight equation (7). The left panel is a 3x3 grid of teal Gaussian-like clusters, which is the base distribution p(x). The middle row is overlaid with dense coral/red samples, which is the reward-tilted target p(x)e^{r(x)}, so the tilt picks out the center row. The right panel shows teal, purple and coral clouds at four corners. Purple and teal are two component distributions p1 and p2. Coral marks the product target p(x) ∝ p1^α p2^β, which sits where the two overlap. Each panel has a boxed legend over the lower-left corner. The eye goes first to the bright coral blobs, then to the equation above.
caption: SMC results for the reward-tilting and product target distributions.
abstract: Discrete diffusion models have become highly effective across various domains. However, real-world applications often require the generative process to adhere to certain constraints. To this end, we propose a Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) framework that enables scalable inference-time control of discrete diffusion models through principled importance weighting and optimal proposal construction. Specifically, our approach derives tractable importance weights for a range of intermediate targets and characterises the optimal proposal, for which we develop two practical approximations: a first-order gradient-based approximation and an amortised proposal trained to minimise the log-variance of the importance weights. Empirical results across synthetic tasks, language modelling, biology design, and text-to-image generation demonstrate that our framework enhances controllability and sample quality, highlighting the effectiveness of SMC as a versatile recipe for scaling discrete diffusion models at inference time.
